Gig Economy
GIG ee-KON-uh-mee
noun (Millennial slang)
From gig, jazz musicians’ slang of the 1920s for a single paid engagement, and economy. The phrase was popularized about 2009, as the financial crisis left many young workers piecing together short-term jobs, and with the rise of app-based platforms: TaskRabbit (2008), Uber (2009), Lyft, DoorDash, Fiverr, Upwork. It describes work organized as independent tasks or contracts rather than steady employment, often without benefits. Millennials, entering the workforce during the Great Recession, became its emblematic workers.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The gig economy is work by the task: driving for an app, delivering food, freelancing projects, a patchwork of short-term jobs instead of a single employer. It offers flexibility and independence, and it often brings insecurity, no benefits, and an endless hustle. Millennials, who came of age in the Great Recession, made it their own. The Christian observation: Scripture says a great deal about work and wages, and much of it applies directly. Work itself is good and commanded: "if any would not work, neither should he eat" (2Th 3:10). Providing for one’s household is a sacred duty: "if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel" (1Ti 5:8). Scripture also speaks sharply to employers and systems that squeeze workers: "Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth" (Jas 5:4); "the labourer is worthy of his hire" (Luk 10:7). Day labourers were the gig workers of the Bible, and the law required that they be paid before sundown (Deu 24:15). The gig economy can be an honourable way to earn and provide, and Christians can work in it with diligence and integrity. But it tempts toward two errors: the anxiety that never rests, and the isolation of work without colleagues or community. A father teaches his son to take honest work wherever it is, to work as unto the Lord, to keep the Sabbath even when the app does not, and to aim at building something stable enough to support a family.

Webster 1828 Definition

Millennial-era term (c. 2009; app platforms) for work by the short-term task or contract; honest labour and provision are commanded (2Th 3:10; 1Ti 5:8), and Scripture also guards the labourer’s wage and rest (Jas 5:4; Deu 24:15).

GIG ECONOMY, n. (Millennial-era term, c. 2009–present) An economy of short-term, freelance, or app-based work rather than permanent employment. Related: gig work, side hustle, freelancer.

Webster (1828), root economy: ECONOMY, noun [Latin oeconomia; Gr. house, and law, rule.] 1. Primarily, the management, regulation and government of a family or the concerns of a household. 2. The management of pecuniary concerns or the expenditure of money. Hence, 3. A frugal and judicious use of money; that management which expends money to advantage, and incurs no waste; frugality in the necessary expenditure of money. It differs from parsimony, which implies an improper saving of expense. […]

Decode for parents: honour honest work of every kind, and help your children aim at stability that can support a family.

Key Scripture

2Th 3:10 — "For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat."

1Ti 5:8 — "But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel."

Jas 5:4 — "Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth."

Luk 10:7 — "And in the same house remain, eating and drinking such things as they give: for the labourer is worthy of his hire. Go not from house to house."

Deu 24:15 — "At his day thou shalt give him his hire, neither shall the sun go down upon it; for he is poor, and setteth his heart upon it: lest he cry against thee unto the LORD, and it be sin unto thee."

Modern Corruption

The gig economy offers flexible honest work, but can breed endless anxiety, isolation, and unprotected labour; Scripture commands work and guards the labourer’s wage and rest.

expand to see more

The corruption is twofold. For workers, gig work can become an unending hustle with no rest, no community, and no future, where the app’s demand never stops and Sabbath becomes impossible. For the system, it can shift risk and cost onto the weakest, paying by the task with no regard for the labourer’s life. Scripture condemns both the idle and the exploiter, and it built rest into the week for servants and day labourers alike.

The recovery is work ordered by God. Christians in the gig economy can work with excellence and honesty, keep the Lord’s Day, and use flexibility for family and church rather than for endless earning. Christians who run businesses should pay fairly and promptly, as the law required for the day labourer. Teach the young that every honest job is a calling, and that the goal of work is not the hustle but faithfulness, provision, and generosity.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

1920s jazz gig (a paid engagement) + Greek oikonomia (household management) → economy → c. 2009 gig economy → app platforms of the 2010s.

1920s: jazz musicians’ gig — a single engagement

c. 2009: gig economy amid the Great Recession

2008–2015: TaskRabbit, Uber, Lyft, DoorDash, Upwork

Biblical anchor: the labourer is worthy of his hire (Luk 10:7); at his day thou shalt give him his hire (Deu 24:15)
